Linking Generations in PSID: A SQL Guide to Family Income Persistence

How income averaging and life stage change estimates of intergenerational family-income persistence

SQL
Python
PSID
Economic Mobility
Seven official PSID files, 187 matched children, and a closer look at how age and income averaging shape estimates of intergenerational persistence.
Author

Yuxi Xie

Published

October 23, 2026

Income measurement changes the mobility story. Averaging both generations’ incomes gives an IGE of 0.302 in early adulthood and 0.489 in midlife (models B and D); separating the measures shows which generation drives the change.

How do we build a reliable parent–child family income table in SQL, and what changes when we measure income at different ages and over several years?

SQL links seven official PSID files into one row per child. Python estimates intergenerational income elasticity (IGE): the percentage difference in child family income associated with a 1% difference in father family income.1

Income always means total family money income. The father link identifies whose family to follow; that family’s income can include the mother or other members. Adult children’s family income can include a partner’s income. The analysis compares two generations’ family resources, not individual wages.

Part I · Build the evidence in SQL

1. Start with people, then add family income

From PSID Packaged Data, use the cross-year Individual File for people and father links, and six Family Files for income.2

Official archive One source row represents Role in this analysis
ind2023er.zip A person, with fields across survey waves Stable identifiers, father pointers, birth years and annual family membership
fam1999er.zip A family unit interviewed in 1999 1998 income: fathers and young adult children
fam2001er.zip A family unit interviewed in 2001 2000 income: fathers and young adult children
fam2003er.zip A family unit interviewed in 2003 2002 income: fathers and young adult children
fam2015er.zip A family unit interviewed in 2015 2014 income: the same children in midlife
fam2017er.zip A family unit interviewed in 2017 2016 income: the same children in midlife
fam2019er.zip A family unit interviewed in 2019 2018 income: the same children in midlife

Python reads the supplied official ZIPs using their SAS column positions: 85,536 people and 50,449 family-wave records (source manifest). The extracted CSVs preserve original fields and values.

This example reads 2000 income from the 2001 Family File; the full parser checks all seven archives.

from pathlib import Path
import io, re, zipfile
import pandas as pd

archive = Path("data/raw/fam2001er.zip")
with zipfile.ZipFile(archive) as z:
    sas = z.read("FAM2001ER.sas").decode("ascii")
    positions = {
        name: (int(start)-1, int(end))
        for name, start, end in re.findall(
            r"\b(\w+)\s+(\d+)\s*-\s*(\d+)", sas
        )
    }
    fields = ["ER17002", "ER20456"]
    with z.open("FAM2001ER.txt") as source:
        raw_2001 = pd.read_fwf(
            io.TextIOWrapper(source, encoding="ascii"),
            colspecs=[positions[v] for v in fields],
            names=fields, header=None
        )
print(raw_2001.sort_values("ER17002").head())

Actual first five rows. ER17002 is the 2001 family interview number; ER20456 is total family income for 2000.

2. Give each table the right key

Use ER30001*1000 + ER30002 as the stable person key. Annual family keys require both the interview number and survey year.3

Working table Row unit Unique key
persons Person person_id
roster Responding person in a survey wave person_id, survey_year
family_income Family unit in a survey wave survey_year, family_interview_id
matched_income Child with all required income measures child_id

From the post folder, load the original columns into SQLite. Preparation SQL creates keys, selects the latest valid birth year and stacks waves with UNION ALL; unique indexes reject duplicates.

from pathlib import Path
import math, sqlite3
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

root = Path.cwd()
con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.create_function("LN", 1, lambda x: math.log(x) if x and x > 0 else None)
con.create_function("EXP", 1, math.exp)
pd.read_csv(root / "data/selected/individual.csv").to_sql(
    "individual_raw", con, index=False
)
for year in [1999, 2001, 2003, 2015, 2017, 2019]:
    pd.read_csv(root / f"data/selected/family_{year}.csv").to_sql(
        f"raw_{year}", con, index=False
    )
con.executescript((root / "sql/01_prepare.sql").read_text())

Run creation statements with con.executescript(sql_text) and display queries with pd.read_sql_query(sql_text, con).

3. Find fathers with a self-join

Father fields ER32016/ER32017 point to another person’s stable ID. A self-JOIN resolves that link; SELECT keeps the required fields.

Follow children born 1972–1976 with fathers 45–60 in 2000 and a birth-year gap of 15–55. Children are approximately 24–28 in 2000 and 40–44 in 2016; father-family-income dates stay fixed.

CREATE TABLE father_child_links AS
SELECT c.person_id AS child_id,p.person_id AS father_id,
       c.birth_year AS child_birth_year,p.birth_year AS father_birth_year,
       c.sex AS child_sex
FROM persons c JOIN persons p ON c.father_id=p.person_id
WHERE c.birth_year BETWEEN 1972 AND 1976
  AND 2000-p.birth_year BETWEEN 45 AND 60
  AND c.birth_year-p.birth_year BETWEEN 15 AND 55;
SELECT child_id, father_id, child_birth_year, father_birth_year
FROM father_child_links
ORDER BY child_id
LIMIT 5;
child_id father_id child_birth_year father_birth_year
4031 4003 1973 1951
4032 4170 1973 1955
4033 4003 1975 1951
4034 4170 1975 1955
4035 4172 1976 1949

The sample audit narrows 4,925 cohort children to 1,878 resolved father links and 1,490 age-eligible pairs.

A LEFT JOIN keeps unmatched roster records visible for the audit.

SELECT r.survey_year, COUNT(*) AS responding_people,
       SUM(f.family_interview_id IS NULL) AS unmatched_family_ids
FROM roster r
LEFT JOIN family_income f
  ON r.survey_year = f.survey_year
 AND r.family_interview_id = f.family_interview_id
GROUP BY r.survey_year;
survey_year responding_people unmatched_family_ids

2001 20423 0

2015 23094 0
2017 24998 0
2019 24699 0

Source: annual roster-to-family join audit. Counts include all responding roster members before the adult-role and income filters.

All roster records match. Next retain reference persons, spouses and partners with positive valid income: this measures each adult’s own family resources and permits logarithms.

CREATE TABLE person_income AS
SELECT r.person_id,r.survey_year,r.survey_year-1 AS income_year,
       r.survey_year-1-p.birth_year AS income_age,r.family_interview_id,
       f.income AS income_nominal,LN(f.income) AS log_income,f.topcoded
FROM roster r JOIN persons p ON p.person_id=r.person_id
JOIN family_income f ON f.survey_year=r.survey_year
                    AND f.family_interview_id=r.family_interview_id
WHERE r.sequence BETWEEN 1 AND 20 AND r.relationship IN (10,20,22)
  AND p.birth_year IS NOT NULL AND f.income>0 AND f.valid_code=1;
SELECT person_id, income_year, family_interview_id, income_nominal
FROM person_income
WHERE person_id = 4031
ORDER BY income_year;
person_id income_year family_interview_id income_nominal
4031 1998 1702 8000
4031 2000 285 37760
4031 2002 1427 40574
4031 2014 1428 45084
4031 2016 6510 3705
4031 2018 6314 9380

The income audit records 42 negative and 485 zero incomes, preserved in source data but excluded from logs. Valid $1 incomes remain; no top-coded record enters the final sample.4

5. Turn annual rows into comparable income measures

GROUP BY creates person-window rows. COUNT(*) checks coverage, AVG(log_income) averages logs, and conditional MAX selects the central year—2000 or 2016.

CREATE TABLE income_summary AS
SELECT person_id,
       CASE WHEN survey_year IN (1999,2001,2003) THEN 'early' ELSE 'midlife' END AS stage,
       COUNT(*) AS n_obs,AVG(log_income) AS log_multi,
       MAX(CASE WHEN survey_year IN (2001,2017) THEN log_income END) AS log_single,
       MAX(CASE WHEN survey_year IN (2001,2017) THEN income_nominal END) AS income_single,
       SUM(topcoded) AS n_topcoded
FROM person_income
GROUP BY person_id,stage;
SELECT person_id, stage, n_obs, log_multi, log_single
FROM income_summary
WHERE person_id IN (4003, 4031, 7035)
ORDER BY person_id, stage
LIMIT 5;
person_id stage n_obs log_multi log_single
4003 early 3 10.754 10.837
4031 early 3 10.046 10.539
4031 midlife 3 9.360 8.217
7035 early 3 10.248 9.889
7035 midlife 3 9.342 8.556

Use 1998/2000/2002 or 2014/2016/2018, without interpolating off-years. Everyone contributes three dates. The mean of logs equals log geometric-mean income, not log arithmetic-mean income.5

6. Make one row per child—and account for exclusions

Join father-early, child-early and child-midlife summaries, requiring n_obs=3 in each. NOT EXISTS excludes pairs sharing an early family unit, preventing a comparison of the same income with itself.

CREATE TABLE common_before_household_check AS
SELECT l.*,p.log_multi AS father_log_multi,p.log_single AS father_log_single,
       y.log_multi AS young_log_multi,y.log_single AS young_log_single,
       a.log_multi AS midlife_log_multi,a.log_single AS midlife_log_single,
       p.n_obs AS father_n,y.n_obs AS young_n,a.n_obs AS midlife_n,
       p.income_single AS father_income_2000,
       y.income_single AS child_income_2000,
       a.income_single AS child_income_2016,
       p.n_topcoded+y.n_topcoded+a.n_topcoded AS n_topcoded
FROM father_child_links l
JOIN income_summary p ON p.person_id=l.father_id AND p.stage='early' AND p.n_obs=3
JOIN income_summary y ON y.person_id=l.child_id AND y.stage='early' AND y.n_obs=3
JOIN income_summary a ON a.person_id=l.child_id AND a.stage='midlife' AND a.n_obs=3;

CREATE TABLE matched_income AS
SELECT m.*,
       EXP(father_log_multi) AS father_income_geo,
       EXP(young_log_multi) AS child_young_income_geo,
       EXP(midlife_log_multi) AS child_midlife_income_geo
FROM common_before_household_check m
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
 SELECT 1 FROM person_income c JOIN person_income p
   ON c.survey_year=p.survey_year AND c.family_interview_id=p.family_interview_id
 WHERE c.person_id=m.child_id AND p.person_id=m.father_id
   AND c.survey_year IN (1999,2001,2003));
SELECT child_id, father_id, father_income_2000,
       child_income_2000, child_income_2016
FROM matched_income
ORDER BY child_id
LIMIT 5;

The matched table contains 187 children and 163 fathers: 109 daughters and 78 sons. Complete-history requirements leave 3.8% of the cohort (\(187/4{,}925\)), so these results describe a selected sample.6

Part II · What the linked table reveals

1. Whose family income is averaged matters

A log–log regression measures the income association between generations, holding the 187-child sample fixed:

\[ \log Y_i^{C,s}=\alpha_s+\beta_s\log Y_i^F+\varepsilon_i, \]

Here \(Y^F\) and \(Y^{C,s}\) are total income in the father’s and adult child’s respective family units; \(s\) is the child’s life stage and \(\beta_s\) the IGE.

Table 1 defines Figure 1’s four models: two child life stages, with either single-year incomes or averages for both generations.

Table 1. Four models, defined by their income years

Model / child stage Father’s family: years Child’s family: years IGE 95% interval
A · Early career 2000 2000 0.285 [0.113, 0.479]
B · Early career 1998 / 2000 / 2002 1998 / 2000 / 2002 0.302 [0.156, 0.461]
C · Midlife 2000 2016 0.311 [0.143, 0.519]
D · Midlife 1998 / 2000 / 2002 2014 / 2016 / 2018 0.489 [0.288, 0.716]

Source: four-model regression results. Income calendar years; A/C use one observation, B/D mean log income. Same 187 children in every model.

Show / hide Python code · estimate the four models 
d = pd.read_sql_query("SELECT * FROM matched_income ORDER BY child_id", con)

def estimate_ige(frame, father_col, child_col):
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(frame)), frame[father_col]])
    return np.linalg.lstsq(X, frame[child_col], rcond=None)[0][1]

specifications = [
    ("Early, single", "father_log_single", "young_log_single"),
    ("Early, mean logs", "father_log_multi", "young_log_multi"),
    ("Midlife, single", "father_log_single", "midlife_log_single"),
    ("Midlife, mean logs", "father_log_multi", "midlife_log_multi"),
]
for label, father_col, child_col in specifications:
    print(label, round(estimate_ige(d, father_col, child_col), 3))

For interpretation, consider two fathers whose families’ measured incomes differ by 10%—an illustrative comparison, not observed income growth. The fitted child-family-income difference is:

\[ \text{Implied child family-income gap (\%)} =100\left[(1.10)^{\hat\beta}-1\right]. \]

Thus model B’s 0.302 implies about \(100[(1.10)^{0.302}-1]=2.9\%\) higher child family income; model D’s 0.489 implies about \(4.8\%\). Table 2 uses unrounded coefficients for all four conversions.

Table 2. What a chosen 10% father-family-income difference implies

Model IGE used Father’s family-income gap Implied child family-income gap
A · Early career 0.285 10% (chosen comparison) 2.75%
B · Early career 0.302 10% (chosen comparison) 2.92%
C · Midlife 0.311 10% (chosen comparison) 3.00%
D · Midlife 0.489 10% (chosen comparison) 4.77%

Source: coefficients from the four-model results, transformed using the displayed formula; calculations saved in the interpretation table. These are fitted cross-family associations, not forecasts or causal effects.

Show / hide Python code · convert slopes into percentage differences 
interpretation = []
for label, father_col, child_col in specifications:
    beta = estimate_ige(d, father_col, child_col)
    interpretation.append({
        "model": label,
        "IGE": beta,
        "chosen_father_difference_pct": 10,
        "implied_child_difference_pct": 100 * (1.10**beta - 1),
    })
print(pd.DataFrame(interpretation).round(3))

The age gap is small with single-year incomes (0.285 versus 0.311) and larger with averages (0.302 versus 0.489).

Age-window differences and uncertainty

Table 3. The age-window difference remains statistically uncertain

Income measure Midlife minus early IGE 95% paired interval
Single year (C − A) 0.026 [-0.161, 0.223]
Both averaged (D − B) 0.187 [-0.008, 0.383]

Source: paired differences and bootstrap intervals. Differences are calculated before rounding the coefficients in Figure 1.

The averaged difference is 0.187, with a 95% paired interval of [−0.008, 0.383]. It includes zero, so the age-window difference is not statistically significant at 5%.7

Table 4 and Figure 2 isolate which generation’s averaging matters.

Show / hide Python code · separate father and child averaging 
factorial = []
for stage in ["young", "midlife"]:
    for father_measure in ["single", "multi"]:
        for child_measure in ["single", "multi"]:
            beta = estimate_ige(
                d, f"father_log_{father_measure}",
                f"{stage}_log_{child_measure}"
            )
            factorial.append([stage, father_measure, child_measure, beta])
comparison = pd.DataFrame(factorial, columns=[
    "stage", "father_measure", "child_measure", "IGE"
])
print(comparison.round(3))

Table 4. Change one generation’s income measure at a time

Child stage Father’s family income Child’s family: single year Child’s family: three observations Change from averaging child’s family income
Early career Single year 0.285 0.194 -0.091
Early career Three observations 0.407 0.302 -0.105
Midlife Single year 0.311 0.315 +0.004
Midlife Three observations 0.508 0.489 -0.019

Source: all eight regression specifications. Read across each row to change only child family income. The last column is averaged minus single-year child IGE; dates follow Table 1.

Averaging the father’s family income raises IGE. Holding child family income to one year, the estimate rises 0.285 → 0.407 in early adulthood and 0.311 → 0.508 in midlife.

Averaging the child’s family income lowers early IGE but barely changes midlife IGE. Across the two fixed father measures, early estimates fall 0.285 → 0.194 and 0.407 → 0.302; midlife estimates change 0.311 → 0.315 and 0.508 → 0.489.

Child averaging therefore offsets much of father averaging’s early-career increase. This fits the distinction between noise in a regressor, which can attenuate a slope, and independent outcome noise, which mainly affects precision; it does not establish a lifetime-income estimate.8

2. Family income fluctuates less in midlife

To assess whether one year’s income is a stable snapshot of family resources, compare the same 187 children across life stages. Subtract each year’s sample mean log income, then calculate each child’s standard deviation across three observations. Smaller values mean less movement relative to the group’s yearly average.

Show / hide Python code · compare each child’s family income fluctuations 
panel = pd.read_sql_query("SELECT * FROM person_income", con)
dispersion = []
for stage, years in [
    ("Early career", [1999, 2001, 2003]),
    ("Midlife", [2015, 2017, 2019]),
]:
    q = panel[panel.person_id.isin(d.child_id)
              & panel.survey_year.isin(years)].copy()
    q["centered_log"] = q.log_income - q.groupby(
        "survey_year"
    ).log_income.transform("mean")
    sd = q.groupby("person_id").centered_log.std()
    dispersion.append(sd.rename(stage))
paired_sd = pd.concat(dispersion, axis=1)
print(paired_sd.median().round(3))
print(round((paired_sd.Midlife < paired_sd["Early career"]).mean(), 3))

The median fluctuation measure falls 0.307 → 0.147, a 52% reduction: \(100(1-\text{midlife median}/\text{early median})\). 129 of 187 children (69%) have smaller midlife fluctuations; Table 5 shows the calculations.

Income-fluctuation calculations

Table 5. Relative family income fluctuates less in midlife for most children

Result Value Calculation
Early-career median income fluctuation 0.307 Median across the same 187 children
Midlife median income fluctuation 0.147 Median across the same 187 children
Reduction in the median 52.1% 100 × (1 − midlife median / early median)
Children with smaller midlife fluctuations 69.0% 100 × 129 / 187

Source: individual dispersion measures; summary calculations. Calculations use unrounded medians. The 52% compares two medians; the 69% counts children with a lower individual value.

Within these windows, a single midlife observation is generally more stable. Fluctuations still include real family-resource changes, so this check does not establish how well an observation represents lifetime income.

Leaving out each father and his children preserves the averaged estimates’ ordering (Table 6).

Leave-one-father sensitivity check

Table 6. The averaged estimates remain ordered when one father is left out

Both-generation averages Lowest leave-one-father IGE Highest leave-one-father IGE
Early career (B) 0.270 0.323
Midlife (D) 0.456 0.525

Source: leave-one-father minimum and maximum columns in the regression results, for the two models averaging both generations. These ranges are sensitivity checks, not confidence intervals.

The pattern fits lifecycle concerns, but period changes and family composition also matter; age alone is not identified.9

Takeaway

SQL turns seven official PSID files into an auditable table of 187 children and 163 fathers. On this fixed sample, averaging fathers’ family income raises IGE; averaging children’s family income lowers early IGE by about 0.10 but barely changes midlife estimates (Table 4). Relative family income also fluctuates less in midlife for 69% of children (Figure 3).

Income measurement changes the mobility story. The averaged IGE rises from 0.302 to 0.489, but its age-window difference remains statistically uncertain (Table 3). Longer histories and broader cohorts would help distinguish lifecycle patterns from period and family changes.

Reproducibility

The analysis code is available in the accompanying project, with SQL preparation, matching queries and Python analysis. Original archives come from the official PSID Packaged Data page; variable definitions are linked in the PSID documentation catalogue.

The standalone project uses the following structure:

index.qmd
README.md
code/                  # extraction, SQL execution, analysis and checks
sql/
├── 01_prepare.sql     # stable keys and annual tables
└── 02_match.sql       # father links and income-window joins
data/
├── raw/               # seven original PSID ZIPs, supplied separately
├── selected/          # unchanged source columns
└── processed/         # generated tables and SQLite database
result/
├── matched_income.csv # final analysis table
├── *.csv              # estimates, calculations and audits
└── figures/           # three 300-dpi PNGs

To rebuild, install requirements.txt and run python code/run_all.py. For fresh extraction, place the seven ZIPs in data/raw/ and first run python code/01_extract_official.py. Copy the whole post folder to blog/posts/post6/ before rendering the website. The README contains the full inventory and commands.

Footnotes

  1. A higher IGE means a closer link between generations’ incomes—and less relative mobility by this measure. “Income” here covers the whole family, including a partner’s income, rather than just one person’s pay.↩︎

  2. The data come from the University of Michigan’s PSID. This analysis uses the seven official files supplied for the project; their versions and record counts are listed in the README.↩︎

  3. A person keeps the same identifier as families change. The father link is recorded in PSID’s individual-file codebook; it is not guessed from who lives together.↩︎

  4. A 2001 interview reports income for 2000. Zero and negative incomes are kept in the source data but left out of the log calculation; PSID’s own imputed values remain. Details are in the data notes.↩︎

  5. The averages use logs, giving less weight to unusually large dollar amounts than a simple dollar average would. Everyone contributes the same dates, so a common annual inflation adjustment would leave these slopes unchanged; nominal dollars still cannot measure changes in purchasing power across the two periods.↩︎

  6. Requiring complete income histories leaves a small, selected group. The results describe these families, without survey weights, rather than all American families.↩︎

  7. The intervals come from repeatedly resampling fathers, keeping siblings together. The age comparison uses each resampled group for both estimates, so it measures uncertainty in their difference directly.↩︎

  8. A good or bad year can make income a misleading guide to longer-run resources. Research by Bhash Mazumder shows why observing more years can matter; averaging does not automatically remove every source of error.↩︎

  9. Steven Haider and Gary Solon find that the age at which earnings are observed affects how well they represent lifetime earnings. Mazumder’s later PSID work uses longer income histories around midlife.↩︎
